source_text: Fragmenta in epistulam ad Romanos Rom 7 Ἀγαθοεργῶν ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος εἰκὼν ἀκηλίδωτος ἐγίνετο τῶν μαθητευομένων, ὅτου χάριν καὶ ἐκέκραξεν· μιμηταί μου γίνεσθε, καθὼς καὶ ἐγὼ Χριστοῦ. τοιγαροῦν οὐκ αὐτοῦ ἐστι κατὰ κυριολεξίαν ὃ ἔφη· οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου τὸ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ τὸ ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου; ἀλλὰ ταῦτα καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ ὑποκρινόμενος λέγει πρὸς ἔλεγχον τῶν φιλαμαρτημόνων. ὥσπερ δὲ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀπὸ τῶν σφῶν πράξεων σαρκικούς, ψυχικούς, πνευματικοὺς καὶ ἑτέροις μυρίοις ὀνόμασι καλεῖν οἶδεν ἡ θεία γραφή, οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸν διάβολον οὐ μόνον σατανᾶν καὶ ἀντικείμενον καὶ διάβολον καὶ ὄφιν καὶ λέοντα καλεῖν οἶδεν καὶ Βελίαρ, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ σάρκα καὶ νόμον καὶ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ θάνατον· τούτοις γὰρ ἐδουλεύσαμεν διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς καὶ οὐ τῷ Χριστῷ. ὅτου χάριν λέγει· ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, δηλῶν ὡς νυνὶ οὐκέτι ὄντων αὐτῶν ἐν σαρκί, καίπερ ὄντων ἐν σαρκί, ὡς οὐκ ἄρα τὴν σάρκα ἣν περικείμεθα διαβάλλων, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὁμωνύμως αὐτῇ λεγομένην σάρκα, ἧς καὶ ἀπηλλάγημεν διὰ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐν Χριστῷ διὰ τοῦ συνταφῆναι αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος. ὄντως ταύτης ἠλευθερώθημεν τῆς σαρκός· ἐπιφέρει γὰρ λέγων· νυνὶ δὲ κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα, ὥστε δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος καὶ οὐ παλαιότητι γράμματος. εἰθ' οὕτως ἤρξατο πάλιν τῆς καθ' ὑπόθεσιν προσωποποιΐας, ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο· ἕως τοῦ ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου; ἄσειστον θεμέλιον προθέμενος ἐν προλόγῳ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπολογίαν οὕτω λέγων· τί οὖν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο, καὶ ὅτι ὁ μὲν 2 νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ ἀγαθή. ἐνταῦθα νόμον λέγει οὐ τὸν ἀντιστρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ νοὸς ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ τὸν προπαραινετικόν, τὸν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας κολάζοντα. ὅτου χάριν καὶ συνεψηφίσατο αὐτῷ ὡς ὁσίῳ καὶ δικαίῳ καὶ ἀγαθῷ. εἰθ' οὕτως ἤρξατο πάλιν ἐπιλύειν ἀκολούθως οἷς ἀνωτέρω προεῖπεν, λόγον εὐχάριστον προοιμιασάμενος οὕτως· εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν. εἶτα πρὸς κατάκρισιν τῶν τοιάδε ἀφορμαζομένων καὶ κακιζόντων ἃς περικείμεθα σάρκας, λέγει ἐπερωτηματικῶς ἆρα οὖν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας; ἆρα κἀγὼ Παῦλος μεμέρισμαι, πῆ μὲν δουλεύων νόμῳ θεοῦ, πῆ δὲ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας; ἆρα τὸν Χριστὸν καὶ τὸν Βελίαρ ἅμα καὶ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔχω ἐν ἐμαυτῷ; ἆρα ἐγὼ ὁ λέγων· ζῶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγώ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός, ψευσάμενος τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ζῶσαν ἔχω ἐν ἐμαυτῷ; ὁ ἄλλοις προσφωνήσας· οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν, καὶ δοξάσατε τὸν θεὸν ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν, αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ σώματι οὐδὲν ἔχων ἀγαθόν; ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔστι τοιοῦτος, οὐκ ἔστιν· μὴ γένοιτο· τέκνον γὰρ ὀργῆς καὶ σκεῦος ὀργῆς πρίν, μεταβαλὼν τὸν τρόπον οὐ τὴν φύσιν, ἐγένετο τίμιον ἐκλογῆς σκεῦος.
thought_title: Paul speaks in a substituted persona, not as himself
orientation: Didymus opens his commentary on Romans 7 by arguing that Paul's words about the wretched man and indwelling sin are spoken in a substituted persona, not about Paul himself or any Christian buried with Christ in baptism.
pass_a_gloss: The divine apostle became an unspotted image of good works for those being taught, for which reason he also cried out: 'Become imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.' Therefore it is not his own, in the proper sense of the word, what he said: 'But I know that good does not dwell in my flesh,' nor indeed the 'Wretched man am I, who will rescue me from the body of this death?' But these things and as many such things he says, speaking in character in a substituted persona, for the refutation of those who love sin. Just as the divine Scripture knows how to call human beings fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and by countless other names from their own actions, so indeed it knows how to call the devil not only Satan and adversary and devil and serpent and lion and Beliar, but also flesh and law and sin and death; for to these we were enslaved through disobedience, and not to Christ. For which reason he says: 'When we were in the flesh,' making clear that now they are no longer in flesh, although they are in flesh, as therefore not slandering the flesh which we wear around us, but the flesh called by the same name as it, from which we also were set free because we died in Christ through being buried with him through baptism. Truly from this flesh we were set free; for he brings in, saying: 'But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that in which we were held, so that we serve in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter.' Then thus he began again the hypothetical speaking in character, beginning from 'What then shall we say? Is the law sin? May it never be!' until 'Wretched man am I, who will rescue me from the body of this death?' Having set before himself an unshaken foundation in the prologue, his own defense, saying thus: 'What then? Is the law sin? May it never be,' and that 'the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.' Here he says law, not the one warring against the law of our mind, but the one that gives prior warning, the one that punishes those who sin. For which reason he also voted together with it as holy and just and good. Then thus he began again to explain in sequence what he had said above, having prefaced a word of thanksgiving thus: 'I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Then, for the condemnation of those who take occasion from such things and speak evil of the flesh which we wear around us, he says interrogatively: 'So then, do I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin?' Am I, Paul, divided, serving the law of God in one respect, but the law of sin in another? Do I have Christ and Beliar at the same time and in the same place in myself? Do I, the one saying: 'But I no longer live, but Christ lives in me,' have sin living in myself, having been shown a liar? The one who addressed others: 'Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit in you, and glorify God in your members,' do I myself have nothing good in my body? But he is not such, he is not; may it never be; for a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath before, having changed his manner, not his nature, he became a precious vessel of election.

lemmas.gloss: speaking in character, playing a part
we have been released, rendered inoperative
interrogatively, in the form of a question

choices.english: speaking in character in a substituted persona
choices.why: The brief's glossary requires 'substituted persona' for παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ and 'speaking in character' for προσωποποιΐα; the participle ὑποκρινόμενος is rendered 'speaking in character' to match the glossary's rhetorical sense.
rejected: playing a part in a substituted person

choices.why: The compound means 'sin-loving'; rendering it as a substantive participle preserves the Greek's compactness and the polemical force.

The participle is passive in sense here: Paul would be exposed as a liar if the hypothetical were true; rendering it as 'having been shown a liar' avoids making Paul the active liar, which the checker flagged as a mistranslation.

choices.term: κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας
choices.english: we have been released from the law of sin
choices.why: The glossary bans 'God's law' and 'the devil's power' for νόμος; 'released' captures καταργέω's sense of being rendered inoperative or discharged from a binding force.
rejected: we have been abolished from the law of sin
we have been made ineffective from the law of sin

choices.english: the one that gives prior warning
choices.why: The adjective means 'admonitory beforehand'; rendering it as a relative clause preserves the contrast with the law warring against the mind and clarifies its function.
rejected: the one that warns in advance

choices.term: συνεψηφίσατο αὐτῷ ὡς ὁσίῳ καὶ δικαίῳ καὶ ἀγαθῷ
choices.english: he also voted together with it as holy and just and good
choices.why: The verb συμψηφίζομαι means to concur or vote with; the metaphor of voting preserves the deliberative force of Paul's agreement with the law's character.
rejected: he also concurred with it as holy and just and good
he also cast his vote with it as holy and just and good

pass_b_english: The divine apostle became an unspotted image for his disciples through his good works, which is why he cried out: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Therefore what he said is not literally about himself: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), nor even “Wretched man that I am, who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Rather, he says these things and all such things speaking in character in a substituted persona, to refute those who love sin. Just as divine Scripture knows how to call human beings fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and by countless other names based on their actions, so too it knows how to call the devil not only Satan, the Adversary, the Slanderer, the Serpent, the Lion, and Beliar, but also flesh, law, sin, and death. For we were enslaved to these through disobedience, and not to Christ. This is why he says: “When we were in the flesh” (Romans 7:5), making clear that they are no longer in the flesh, even though they are in the flesh—so he is not slandering the flesh we wear, but the flesh called by the same name, from which we have also been set free because we died in Christ by being buried together with him through baptism. We have truly been set free from this flesh. For he adds: “But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter” (Romans 7:6). Then he began again the hypothetical speaking in character, starting from “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not!” (Romans 7:7) up to “Wretched man that I am, who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Having laid down an unshakable foundation in his preface, he gives his defense in this way: “What then? Is the law sin? Certainly not!” (Romans 7:7), and that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). Here he means by law not the one warring against the law of our mind, but the one that admonishes beforehand and punishes those who sin. This is why he also assented to it as holy and just and good. Then he began again to explain in sequence what he had said earlier, prefacing it with a word of thanksgiving: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). Then, to condemn those who use such things as a pretext and revile the flesh we wear, he says in the form of a question: “So then, do I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin?” Am I, Paul, divided, serving the law of God in one part and the law of sin in another? Do I have Christ and Beliar in myself at the same time and in the same place? Am I, the one who says “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20), having lied, do I have sin living in me? I who proclaimed to others, “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you” (1 Corinthians 6:19), and “Glorify God in your members” (1 Corinthians 6:20)—do I myself have nothing good in my body? But he is not such a person; he is not. Certainly not! For though he was formerly a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath, he changed his manner, not his nature, and became a precious vessel of election.

edits.new: the one that admonishes beforehand and punishes those who sin

fixed: The English 'the one that admonishes beforehand, the one that punishes those who sin' does not misstate the source; it renders both participles (τὸν προπαραινετικόν, τὸν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας κολάζοντα) accurately. However, the suggested fix is a smoother English phrasing, so I made the smallest change to join the two descriptors with 'and'.

dismissed.why: προπαραινετικόν means 'giving commands/instructions beforehand,' not merely admonishing; it refers to the law's prescriptive function.
dismissed.note: προπαραινετικόν means 'advising beforehand', so 'admonishes beforehand' is accurate.

dismissed.why: The Greek participle is causal or concessive ('if I lied'/'since I lied'), not temporal; the rhetorical question asks if Paul was lying when he claimed Christ lives in him.
dismissed.note: The participle sense of 'having lied' is fine; the clumsy 'Am I ... do I' frame of the sentence lies outside this quote and cannot be fixed within it.
